title: Lane on what would turn demand for euros into demand for European safe assets
summary: Philip Lane sees room for a larger international role for the euro while expecting the dollar to remain the dominant international currency. The binding constraint in his argument is the supply of euro assets that investors can hold and hedge at scale. A shift in sentiment towards the dollar can move EUR/USD immediately. Creating a sufficiently liquid European safe asset requires decisions on fiscal backing, issuance and market infrastructure that an exchange-rate move cannot deliver. His 9 January speech therefore offers two distinct propositions for investors: demand for euro exposure may have shifted in 2025, and the structure of European capital markets will determine how much of that shift Europe can retain.

The starting point is the value of scale within monetary union. Lane treats geopolitical fragmentation, technological change, ageing and climate change as substantially common shocks, while acknowledging differences between member states. Common policy can coordinate a response. A larger currency area also gives firms greater scope to invoice in domestic currency. Chart 1 relates the share of exports sent to the euro area to the share invoiced in euros, averaged over 1999–2023. The association is positive with considerable dispersion. Commodities, often invoiced in dollars, are an important exception. Common payment infrastructure spreads fixed development costs. Denmark’s use of Eurosystem platforms to settle payments in krone shows that economies outside the currency union can share some of these benefits (pp. 1–3, notes 1–3).

Scale also changes the economics of funding. Money-market participants, bond investors and banks can hold claims across member states without adding intra-area currency risk. Greater depth can support hedging markets, attract foreign issuers and facilitate supranational borrowing. Integration can nevertheless reverse under stress. Lane attributes the stronger architecture since the 2008–13 crises to several changes, including bank capital, common supervision and resolution, fiscal backstops and the ECB’s facilities for addressing liquidity and transmission risks. Chart 2 shows differing histories of price integration across market segments. Chart 3 compares ten-year sovereign yields with Bunds through 2 January 2026. Lower spread volatility in recent years is consistent with a greater influence of common factors, while the residual spreads still matter to an investor seeking a single safe asset.

The evidence for a change in international demand is more recent and more conditional. In the second quarter of 2025 the euro rose from about $1.08 to $1.18, roughly 9%. The largest quarterly increase in the foreign debt investment flows shown in Chart 6 was also in that quarter. A staff model attributes much of the exchange-rate appreciation to relative risk sentiment. Its identification uses sign restrictions on exchange rates, yields, output and inflation, with some end-sample GDP inputs projected. It cannot say precisely how much of the change was a loss of confidence in the dollar versus greater confidence in the euro. European investors might also retain dollar securities and hedge more of the currency exposure. That distinction matters for translating a currency view into a view on bond flows (Charts 6–7).

Foreign firms can supply euro-denominated claims too. The largest international euro bond deal shown for 2024 was TD Bank’s, worth $5.962 billion on the table’s common reporting basis. DSV’s euro loan was worth $15.598 billion. Chart 8 separately records cumulative net euro bond issuance by non-area companies and shows unusually strong issuance in 2025 through November. None of these quantities measures the supply of a common sovereign safe asset. Bunds provide that service, but Lane considers their outstanding stock too small. The existing volume of common EU debt is also insufficient to support the repo and derivatives markets he envisages. Good credit quality alone cannot supply stress-period liquidity.

One route is joint borrowing for shared expenditure such as defence. Another, attributed to Blanchard and Ubide, would dedicate national revenue to servicing common bonds whose proceeds buy existing national debt. Their example puts common issuance at 25% of GDP. At average interest costs of 2–4%, the annual revenue allocation would amount to 0.5–1% of GDP. That illustrates the governance trade-off between building liquidity and surrendering control of revenues. A separate proposal would tranche portfolios of national bonds, creating a senior claim without the same revenue structure. Both require sufficient scale and credible national fiscal discipline. Lane closes by reaffirming the symmetric 2% inflation target and a response conditioned on a shock’s origin, size and persistence. The proposals are options for Europe’s financial architecture. They carry no commitment on issuance dates or the next ECB rate decision (pp. 11–15).

questions.question: How much of the 2025 currency move reflected a durable change in investors’ holdings?
questions.detail: The speech documents a large exchange-rate move and concentrated quarterly inflows, while allowing for increased hedging of existing dollar holdings. Those mechanisms imply different demand for euro sovereign duration. Start with the balance-of-payments and international-investment-position series cited under Chart 6, separating transactions from valuation effects. Compare these with contemporaneous hedging evidence before treating a level change in EUR/USD as a recurring flow.

questions.question: At what issuance scale would common debt deliver a better stress hedge?
questions.detail: Lane gives a worked fiscal example but no estimate of the issuance threshold for deep dealer, derivatives and repo markets. For a Bund-versus-EU-bond allocation, compare issue size, bid–ask spreads, repo terms and relative price performance during stress in matched maturities. Consult EU debt-management releases and the safe-asset work cited in notes 8–10, keeping credit backing separate from the liquidity value of each instrument.

questions.question: Would additional international euro demand lower the cost of capital for European firms?
questions.detail: Chart 8 includes borrowing by firms outside the currency union. More euro issuance could deepen the currency market while leaving domestic corporate financing little changed. Compare the issuer domicile, funding purpose and investor base of new deals with matched funding costs for European issuers. The ECB securities database underlying Chart 8 and issuer disclosures would help trace which balance sheets receive the financing.
